# ChatMember Empty Fallback Decision Record

This record began with the investigation entry point for the `Update` object. The path is `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/Update.java`, the file belongs to `org.telegram.telegrambots.meta.api.objects`, and the file header shows `JsonProperty`, `AllArgsConstructor`, and `EqualsAndHashCode`. At the time, we did not conclude from this that the member-type implementation was here; we only used it as an entry point to revisit the object's adjacency relationships.

## The 2023-04-19 Issue

The server may add a `ChatMember` state not yet recognized locally. The earlier record conflated "unable to select a specific member type" with "the entire update is unusable," so it first discussed whether deserialization should abort when an unknown value appears.

Three directions were listed:

- Fail outright, so new states surface as early as possible;
- Create a generic member object and retain some fields initially;
- Do not create a concrete member object; limit the impact to the member information itself.

Direct failure is the easiest way to detect changes, but it may also affect other fields in the same update. A generic object seems to preserve information, but in practice it has no stable member-state semantics. The third option would lose details about the unknown state, but would not misidentify it as an existing type.

The initial draft provisionally follows the third option. Known states should not change because of the unknown branch, and an unknown state should not be forced into a known member type. The exact annotation configuration and the result visible to callers are deferred to the next review.

# ChatMember Null Fallback Decision Record

## 2023-04-19: Initial trade-offs

This first surfaced at the object-layer entry point for `Update`. The earlier investigation path was `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/Update.java`. We can confirm that the package name here is `org.telegram.telegrambots.meta.api.objects`, and the file header includes dependencies such as `JsonProperty`, `AllArgsConstructor`, and `EqualsAndHashCode`. This is a useful place to revisit how the update object connects to member information, but file location alone cannot establish where type dispatch belongs.

The question at the time was: if the server added a `status` with no local model, would existing member states still be read as before, or would the entire update fail? The earlier position did not distinguish a missing member object from an invalid update object, so we first laid out the scope of impact.

There were three options. First, fail directly on an unknown value. This would make upstream changes very visible, but would spread a problem with one member field to the entire update. Second, retain a generic object and leave unknown fields for callers to interpret. This would require a separately defined field set and could lead callers to treat an object with no semantic guarantees as a normal member. Third, do not create a concrete member object for an unknown value. This cannot preserve the full details of the unknown state, but it avoids pretending that an existing subtype still applies.

The initial draft chose the third option as a provisional direction. The decision had not yet been reflected in the annotations or deserialization results. Only two preferences were confirmed: the compatibility branch should not alter known mappings, and unknown values should not take on the meaning of known types.

## 2023-07-31: Review addendum

The review treated `status` and the presence of a member object as separate questions. `status` is the discriminator used to select a member subtype, not an ordinary optional property. When discrimination fails, the caller sees no member object it can use as a known type; this does not mean we can assert that the server sent no member-related content.

This review did not support the earlier idea of "marking the entire `Update` as unusable." The update object may still contain fields unrelated to member state, so discarding everything because of an unknown value in one part would have too broad an impact. A generic placeholder object was also left out of the design because it has no clear field contract and would introduce ambiguity into the type branches.

Keep this easy-to-reproduce counterexample: if an unknown state is mapped to an existing subtype, callers will use that type to read fields they assume are present. The program appears to have obtained an object, but it has actually interpreted a new state as an old one. By contrast, the absence of a concrete object forces paths that depend on member semantics to confront the gap.

The review left open whether callers also need separate diagnostics for unknown states once the model layer has chosen a compatibility result. That question involves log placement and business dependencies, and will not be decided in this record. Next time, continue checking the dispatch settings on the type declaration, then revisit the area around where `Update` is read.

Readers usually enter through `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/Update.java`. The file belongs to `org.telegram.telegrambots.meta.api.objects`, and the file header shows `JsonProperty`, `AllArgsConstructor`, and `EqualsAndHashCode`. This is enough to establish that it is a navigation point on the update-object side; it cannot by itself prove that the member-type dispatch configuration is here.

## 2023-04-19: Questions first noted beside the entry point

The earliest wording called the issue a type-dispatch problem involving `ChatMember`, while also describing it as a `Update` field issue. The two descriptions were not distinguished at the time. The actual concern was: when the server provides a member `status` that the local model does not yet recognize, how far will the read operation proceed before stopping?

The old position had an implicit premise: once the member status could not be recognized, there was no value in continuing to process the entire update. This premise had no example to support it, but it affected the ordering of options in the initial draft. The only facts that could initially be confirmed were the object-layer entry point and the boundary represented by an unknown discriminator value; the complete call relationship still could not be inferred from the file location of `Update.java`.

The candidate options were then ordered by risk.

1. Fail deserialization when it encounters an unknown value. The advantage is that changes become immediately visible, making maintainers less likely to mistakenly believe that the local model covers every server-side state. The disadvantage is that the failure propagates along the update-read path, and fields unrelated to member status may also be blocked.
2. Add a generic member object. It can preserve part of the original shape, with the caller making the determination afterward. The disadvantage is that the source of the field boundaries is unclear, and the type name cannot express the semantics of an unknown state; if it enters an existing member branch, misinterpretation becomes less obvious.
3. Do not create a concrete known member object for an unknown value. The details of the unknown state will not naturally land in an existing model, but the impact can remain at the member-object layer.

The initial draft leaned toward the third direction, but did not treat "no object value" as an already-implemented interface behavior. That version recorded only the trade-offs: known types must not be changed by a new branch, and unknown types must not borrow the meaning of an old type. The implementation location, null-value form, and handling by business callers were left for later review.

## 2023-07-31: Separating the three layers after review

When the second addition was made, the review first asked what role `status` actually serves. It is not an ordinary field, but a discriminator value used to select a member subtype. When the discriminator value is not in the local set, the issue first occurs at the step of "which object to select"; it is not a judgment about whether `Update` exists, nor a business decision about whether to consume the entire update.

This separation rolled back the overly broad failure tendency in the initial draft. If an unknown member status causes the entire `Update` to fail, the caller loses content unrelated to the member status. That cost cannot be offset merely by "making upstream changes easier to detect," because detecting changes and interrupting by default are two separate goals. The model layer can avoid misclassification, and business paths that truly depend on member status can then decide whether they need to refuse to continue.

The same review also rejected a generic placeholder model. There is no answer as to where the placeholder object's fields come from. Keeping only common fields would make callers think that the unknown state already has stable support; retaining all fields would amount to exposing another model without a model contract. If this unknown state is later made into a formal subtype, the migration relationship between the placeholder object and the formal type would also need to be reinterpreted.

A practical boundary judgment from the review is retained here: the server sending member-related data does not mean that the local side can necessarily select a supported subtype for it. An object missing from the caller's view cannot be taken as evidence that the upstream side sent no data; likewise, seeing an object-layer result does not mean that the business logic already understands this new state.

## Review examples: two opposite misreadings

The later review did not try to list every member state, but retained two examples pointing in opposite directions.

The first example treats unknown `status` as the closest existing state. The superficial result looks best: the caller still receives an object, and the existing branch can continue running. But the object type itself has already conveyed the wrong semantics. Code that depends on that type may read a field that is valid only for the old state; the problem will not surface at dispatch, but will be delayed until a business decision or output result.

The second example treats the unknown state as an exception for the entire update. It avoids misidentification, but expands a local gap into failure of the object as a whole. Even other readable content in the update is discarded along with it. This example shows that the broadest possible interruption cannot be adopted merely to preserve "no misclassification."

The boundary left by these two examples is: an unknown state can neither masquerade as a known state nor automatically declare the entire update invalid. The model layer only needs to provide a member result that is not misleading; whether to continue using other fields depends on the caller's own dependencies.

## Overturned old passage

The old on-call note once contained the following judgment:

> An unrecognized member status may contaminate subsequent processing, so the caller should stop consuming the current update.

The original passage is not deleted; it is marked alongside as "Later overturned." It reflects the early misreading that treated the member object and the update object as the same failure boundary. The issue is not that an unknown state has no risk, but that the scope of the risk was not bounded. Paths that require member-state semantics may choose to stop, but the object layer should not make this expanded decision on behalf of every caller.

The same old note also left a troubleshooting order: first confirm whether `Update` is empty, then treat the unknown member state as an exception for the entire object, and finally have the caller catch the deserialization failure. This order is also marked as "Deprecated." Checking `Update` itself cannot explain why member dispatch did not produce a supported type; handing the exception to every caller would cause inconsistent handling of the same object-layer issue.

Keeping the old passage also serves another purpose: it explains why the later decision was not made solely on the basis that "failure is more conspicuous." The old sequence squeezed the entry point, discriminator, result, and business action into a single step, making it easy when reading the code to jump directly from the file path to a conclusion about responsibility.

## Limitations left when looking back from `Update.java`

`Update.java` remains a valid trace-back entry. Readers can use the object-adjacent location to confirm how member information is put into the update object, and can continue looking for related types through packages and direct declarations. However, the old troubleshooting record mistakenly rewrote "the issue name and call name point to this file" as "this file determines all fallback behavior"; that wording is no longer used.

The revised code-reading order is narrower: first confirm the member-type discriminator configuration, then return to `Update.java` to inspect the adjacency of the member-information read; only when the issue clearly involves business dependencies should the caller be traced further. This order is not a generally applicable troubleshooting procedure, but only the location relationship retained by this decision.

The dependencies in the file header can also serve only as local clues. `JsonProperty` can indicate that the object definition uses property mapping, and the Lombok annotations can indicate that constructor- and equality-related declarations exist, but neither can by itself explain what result an unknown state should become. Someone once treated these annotations and the path together as evidence of implementation responsibility; that inference was later withdrawn during review.

## Review addendum before 2025-06-26

A later addendum rechecked the compatibility costs of the three options. The direct-failure option converts "the server-side type set expands" into "reading the current update fails"; the generic-object option converts "there is no local model" into "the caller receives a seemingly usable new type"; and the default-fallback option confines the unknown member to a result without the semantics of a known subtype.

The review did not interpret the default fallback as complete support. It resolves only two runtime issues: known states continue to use the existing mapping, and unknown states must not be misclassified. The raw fields of an unknown object do not thereby automatically enter the member model, and a caller that depends on that state does not acquire its business semantics merely by receiving an absent result.

One adjacent question remains unresolved here: does the caller need to distinguish between "this field originally had no member object" and "an unknown `status` exists, but the local side did not form a usable member object"? The existing record has not established a unified log field, diagnostic location, or business interface, so this page cannot casually turn the question into a rule. This is a matter of visibility and caller conventions; it does not change the fallback boundary already determined at the object layer.

## Meeting and review traces

Several discussions consistently centered on the same disagreement: is failure more effective than absence at reminding maintainers? The final judgment was not an either-or slogan, but a separation of alerting from interruption. If business logic must depend on a particular member status, it needs to identify that dependency where it is used; the model layer should not fabricate a type to improve visibility, nor should it mark the entire update as bad data because of an unknown state.

The review also required the record to preserve the distinction between "unknown" and "no data." An unknown state may correspond to a complete object already sent by the server, with the local side simply lacking an available concrete model; no data may mean that the update originally contained no member information. The current material is insufficient to define an additional diagnostic interface for these two cases, so this page records only the distinction and does not claim that a unified marker already exists.

Another meeting trace is the downgrade of the `Update` entry: it was changed from "suspected implementation location" back to "object-adjacency navigation." The path was not deleted because it can still help future maintainers find the relevant checkpoint from the update object; only the claim that responsibility could be inferred directly from the location was removed.

## Current decision

In `ChatMember`, unknown `status` variants must be decoded as `null` according to `JsonTypeInfo.defaultImpl = Void.class`; known subtypes continue to be handled using the existing mapping.

This sentence turns the early "no object value" into an explicit object-layer result. The `null` here means that the unknown variant did not form a supported `ChatMember` subtype; it is not a new member state, does not carry the unknown object's fields, and is not a failure marker for the entire `Update`. Known subtypes continue to use the existing mapping; the known path must not be rewritten merely to catch the unknown branch.

The relationship between the current position and the old options can be shown as follows:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Dispatch
    Dispatch --> KnownSubtype : known status
    Dispatch --> NullResult : unknown status
    KnownSubtype --> UpdateRead
    NullResult --> UpdateRead
```

The `UpdateRead` in the diagram only indicates that the object-layer result returns to the update-read adjacency; it does not mean that every business caller must continue processing. The raw details of the unknown state are not saved as a generic object by this decision; if a formal subtype is added later, its own mapping should be added rather than leaving it permanently in the default fallback.

## Adjacent issues not yet separated out

This decision does not specify a log field, alert location, or unified caller interface for unknown states. For paths that require member status for a strong business decision, whether the absence caused by an originally missing member object and the absence caused by unknown `status` must be recorded separately remains for another local decision. The object-layer `null` result cannot serve as the answer to this question.

Nor does the location of `Update.java` establish caller responsibility. That path is retained only as a trace-back entry; the member-type discriminator configuration, the update-object read adjacency, and the actual business branch remain three distinct checkpoints. When adding a model later, first confirm whether the new state already has a formal subtype, and then decide whether the mapping should change.

## Appendix of old examples

### Old Example One: Writing an Unknown Value as an Ordinary Member

An early example treated an unrecognized state as an ordinary member object and then had the caller infer the difference from whether the fields were empty. This example is deprecated. An empty field cannot correct the wrong semantics already conveyed by the object type; instead, it may allow the normal branch to continue using incorrect assumptions.

### Old Example Two: Using an Update Exception as an Upstream-Change Signal

Another old example suggested treating an update-read failure as a change signal whenever the member status could not be recognized. This method is indeed more conspicuous, but it also discards readable content unrelated to the member status and does not fit the later-defined impact scope, so it remains as a historical counterexample.

### Old Example Three: Assigning All Responsibility Based on File Location

There was also an old example that never became a formal proposal: since the investigation began at `Update.java`, the member model, fallback strategy, and business handling were all assigned to this file. It never became a decision, but it once changed the direction of the investigation. The path is still retained, but is acknowledged only as providing object-adjacency navigation.

### Old Example Four: Using a Generic Placeholder Object to Postpone the Decision

The generic placeholder object also remains in the appendix. It defers the field-retention issue to the caller, but does not explain which fields are reliable or which type checks are valid. This option was not adopted; that does not mean that no unknown object may preserve raw content. It only means that this `ChatMember` decision does not use a member type with no stable semantics in place of the dispatch result.

These old examples have not been rewritten as the current truth. They preserve two early misjudgments: interpreting the unknown too broadly, or penalizing a local unknown too severely. The current decision is confined to the member-type decoding boundary; other adjacent issues continue to be handled according to their own materials.

# User Capability Field Trial Plan

This round, treat the two types of capabilities on User as inputs that can coexist. Don't preemptively require at the API layer that one must be absent when the other is present. The main Web App capability and the business connection capability come from different usage scenarios; after receiving a User, callers should be able to retain the capability information they received, then decide whether to display an entry point.

The initial draft considered two approaches: add separate properties and validate each independently, or first put both values through a single object round trip to check that neither is dropped when the object is read and then written back out. The latter is preferred because it can expose object-layer overwrites earlier.

For now, the inspection starting point is `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/message/Message.java`. This shows a nearby example of an object model using Jackson annotations; it does not establish where User is implemented or where its fields belong.

If the dual-capability sample causes an existing capability to disappear, first stop the combined round-trip experiment and retain single-field validation. Decide whether the two capabilities need to use the same construction path once real caller samples are available.

# User Capability Field Trial Plan

After review, the initial draft's wording, "process them together first," is too broad. The goal isn't to merge the two capabilities into one abstract flag, but to ensure that a single User object retains each capability's state between reading and writing. Both capabilities can be meaningful to a caller at the same time; the presence or absence of one cannot be used as a proxy for the other.

This round keeps two experiment tracks.

- Single-capability sample: provide only the main Web App capability and check that both the read result and the object written back out still carry that capability.
- Combined sample: include both capabilities and check that the two values remain distinguishable after reading and that the output retains both keys.

We previously considered a separate object-conversion path for the business connection capability. We aren't pursuing that approach at this stage: it would route the combined sample around the main path, masking exactly the loss we're trying to find. Another option is to collapse all capabilities into a generic collection; the available material doesn't establish that callers need this shape, and it would also alter the readability of existing objects, so it is not a goal for this round either.

Source inspection still starts at `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/message/Message.java`. `Message` is in the message object package, its class declaration implements `MaybeInaccessibleMessage`, and the file has visible imports for `JsonIgnore`, `JsonIgnoreProperties`, and `JsonProperty`. This only helps confirm that objects in this area use annotations to handle JSON names; User's fields and accessors must be checked separately on the actual object.

The withdrawal criteria are also more specific: if the combined sample can retain only one capability, or if the two capabilities can no longer be distinguished after writing, do not submit that implementation for compatibility closeout. The single-capability experiment's results can still be retained, but must not be treated as evidence that coexistence has been established.

Two points remain undecided: whether callers depend on the distinction between null values and missing fields, and whether public accessor naming will affect existing compilation results. Both need to be settled in the context of actual usage.

# User Capability Field Trial Plan

The initial draft focused on "whether both use the same conversion path." On review, that is not the right criterion. What actually causes problems for callers is one capability overwriting the other after an object round-trips through JSON, or the reader incorrectly treating the two capabilities as mutually exclusive. There is no need to create a new capability set here, and the business connection capability should not stand in for the main Web App capability.

This plan uses an incremental field approach: retain the separate public accessors and JSON names, and make combined samples a required pre-submission check. Single-capability samples are still useful, but they only show that the individual field has not been lost; only combined samples can reveal overwrites, aliasing, or incorrect mutual-exclusion branches on the same User.

## What This Revision Changes

The previous draft presented a "shared object path" as if it were an implementation decision. That would direct attention to internal structure, whereas callers actually see the User's properties and values. The two capabilities are no longer required to use the same internal fields or the same construction steps; they must remain separately accessible after the object is read and written.

The nearby `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/message/Message.java` can serve as a starting point for looking up annotation style. That file is in the message package; the class declaration for `Message` is `public class Message implements MaybeInaccessibleMessage {`, and the file imports Jackson annotations such as `JsonProperty`. Someone previously used this as the basis for treating Message as the place to add the User fields. That conclusion is not valid: it only shows that the JSON annotation is used within the same object module, and cannot substitute for checking User itself.

## Trial Scope

First, prepare two types of object input: one with only the main Web App capability, and one with both the main Web App and business connection capabilities. For each type of input, perform one read and one serialization, then inspect the output object. During these checks, do not infer field presence from UI, or use whether a capability's business entry point is enabled as a substitute for the object result.

Check the combined samples in this order:

1. After the read, the User exposes both capabilities, rather than retaining only the one processed last.
2. After reserialization, both corresponding keys are still present, and their values have not been renamed or overwritten.
3. Call Fang Ke to make separate decisions based on the two accessors; there is no need to derive an "overall capability" first.

Single-capability samples are only for isolating problems. If the single-capability samples pass but the combined samples fail, first check the relationships between object fields, accessors, and the JSON mappings; do not attribute the problem to either capability itself. Conversely, passing the combined samples does not automatically mean that all historical User samples are covered. This round has not established full compatibility for missing fields, old server responses, or other capability fields.

## Current Interface Requirements

`User.getHasMainWebApp()` must be available; the JSON property `has_main_web_app` accepts `Boolean.TRUE` and preserves that key and value during serialization.

`User.getCanConnectToBusiness()` must be retained alongside `getHasMainWebApp()`; `can_connect_to_business` and `has_main_web_app` can both be deserialized as true in the same object.

These two statements define the external contract for closing out this round. They do not require the two capability values to be equal, nor do they allow one accessor's result to stand in for the other. For combined input, both the read result and the written output should expose two independent decision points to callers.

## Trade-offs and Rollback

Making the business connection capability a derived state of the main Web App capability was considered. That would make single-capability samples shorter, but would inherently leave no place to represent combined inputs and prevent callers from distinguishing the business entry points, so it was rejected. Introducing a generic capability container first, with accessors then reading values from that container, was also considered. There is not enough caller-side evidence to support that direction; at this stage it would only expand the scope of changes, so it is left for later discussion.

If any of the following happens during a combined round-trip, this round's implementation should be rolled back rather than just changing the test expectations: only one accessor is available after the read; the output retains only one JSON key; or, when both keys are present, one capability's value is overwritten by the other. During rollback, the local changes to the single-field accessors can be retained as a draft pending validation, but we cannot claim that the business connection capability coexists compatibly with the main Web App capability.

Still to be confirmed: how callers distinguish missing fields from null values, and whether any integration code depends on the old object serialization order. For error handling of identity fields, see DOC-13; this page does not expand the scope to a migration plan covering every User field.

# User Identity Field Compatibility Troubleshooting Tree

### Early Notes: Messages First

The earliest investigation started with `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/message/Message.java`. The only description available was "the identity identifier looks unchanged, but the caller reports inconsistent reads"; not enough input snippets had been retained. At the time, the message container was the default starting point: if the message existed, check the associated user; if the associated user was visible, provisionally treat the field issue as a discrepancy outside the object.

The old tree is still here to show why messages were checked first at the time:

```text
Message-related identity issues
├─ Message does not exist
│  └─ Confirm whether the input is actually on the message path
├─ Message exists, associated user is not visible
│  └─ Record the input shape; stop at the message decoding boundary
└─ Associated user is visible
   └─ Provisionally assume the identity field has been handled within the object
```

This tree only answers "does the input at hand contain a message container?" It does not answer where the read value comes from, or whether the property is retained when the object is written back out. The early notes conflated these questions into a single stopping condition; the problem only became apparent during a later review.

The declaration visible in the message file is:

```java
public class Message implements MaybeInaccessibleMessage {
```

It is in the `org.telegram.telegrambots.meta.api.objects.message` package. The file header contains `JsonIgnore`, `JsonIgnoreProperties`, and `JsonProperty`, so this was once treated as a shared starting point for annotations and the message model. That was not proof of where the user object implementation belonged; the investigation was simply following the files that could be found.

### Review Addendum: Reading a Numeric Value Does Not Mean Output Is Correct

The later review split the report into two sides: the identifier obtained when reading the object, and the properties left after the object was written out as JSON. The message path remains one possible input source, but it can no longer stand in for these two checks.

During one review, the object log showed that the numeric value was present, but there was no output snippet available for comparison. Someone initially suggested attributing this to the message object being replaced after decoding. That claim had no support from the original input and did not cover cases where a user object was received directly, so no field types or annotations were changed. The record kept only three observable items: the original input, the read result, and the JSON written back out.

If the input is not a message container, do not fabricate a `Message` layer and then continue. When an object comes in directly, first save its input shape, then record the read result; only when the message source is clear should the record also state whether the message exists and whether the associated user is visible. An empty message does not automatically mean an identity field issue, and a visible associated user does not automatically mean the round trip is correct.

### On-Call Branches

```text
Report of an anomalous identity value
│
├─ Can the input be confirmed as coming from Message?
│  ├─ Yes
│  │  ├─ Message or associated user is missing
│  │  │  └─ Save the input shape; stop near message decoding
│  │  └─ Both are visible
│  │     └─ Move on to the read value and JSON output
│  └─ No, or the input is a direct user object
│     └─ Skip the message branch
│
├─ Has the original input been retained?
│  ├─ No
│  │  └─ Mark as insufficient input evidence; do not change fields
│  └─ Yes
│     └─ Compare `id` in the input with the read result
│
└─ Can JSON output be obtained?
   ├─ Yes
   │  └─ Check separately whether `id` is present
   └─ No
      └─ Record only the read side; draw no round-trip conclusion
```

"Input shape" here does not mean a fixed set of fields. It only indicates whether the material at hand is a message container, a user within a message, or a direct user object. If `id` is absent from the input, stop on the input side; only when the property is present in the input but the read result is inconsistent should a decoding-boundary record be made. A correct read does not justify skipping the output check, and seeing the property in the output does not prove that the read itself was correct.

### Blanks Left During Review

This round did not merge reports from outside the message path back into the old tree. Direct user objects and users within messages may both carry identity fields, but they reach the investigator in different ways. If the source is already known to be a direct object, the record only needs the input, read result, and output; adding whether a message exists would just make the collected material look like a different type of input.

Output snippets must not be recorded as just "normal" or "abnormal," either. If a snippet is available, it must at least show whether `id` is still present; if it is unavailable, the blank itself is the result. Previously, marking "the log has a value" as complete actually hid the fact that the output had not been retained. The Jackson annotations in the file header should not stand in for that missing output, because annotations appearing in a message file do not mean this object has been written out as expected.

One judgment remains unresolved: if the input and read result have both been retained, but the output is available only as the caller's description, with no object snippet, should the investigation continue into the caller's comparison logic? The existing records contain nothing on the caller's storage of the identifier, so that part should not yet be written up as a message-model issue. On-call notes should stop at "output not obtained," rather than interpreting the missing snippet as a serialization failure.

### Old Margin Notes Kept in Place

> If the user object in the message is not null, provisionally assume the identity field has no compatibility issue.

Early on, this sentence helped rule out one class of null-object cases, but it can no longer serve as a stopping condition. It leaves out direct user objects and the differences between reading and writing. It is being kept because some people still use the old troubleshooting entry point; a note should be added beside it: a visible user object only means observation can continue, not that compatibility has been confirmed.

New capability fields were once suspected of changing the identity field. That guess came from the two kinds of object changes appearing in the same closeout round, not from retained object snippets. The available material does not establish a causal link between the two, so do not treat capability fields as the default explanation for read or output issues.

A minimal input sample is still missing. The next time a report comes in, prioritize bringing back the input, the read result, and the JSON output; if any of the three is missing, stop at the corresponding branch.

It is in the `org.telegram.telegrambots.meta.api.objects.message` package, and the file header contains `JsonIgnore`, `JsonIgnoreProperties`, `JsonProperty`. These details are enough to explain why the old record used `Message` as a navigation point: the message model and Jackson annotations are both right there. They do not indicate that the identity object can only be constructed through a message, nor do they assign the reading or output of user fields to this class.

## 2023-03-20: A Record Starting from the Message Container

The first version's account of the situation was narrowly scoped: first determine whether a message exists, then determine whether a user object is visible near the message. At that time, there was no raw JSON, no snippet of the object after it was output again, and no sample that could distinguish between a "user inside a message" and a "direct user object". So the record treated visible user adjacency as a relatively strong signal and left the remaining differences to the caller.

The original tree is below. The last branch was later crossed out, but the first two branches can still help identify an incorrect entry point:

```text
Message-related identity anomalies
├─ Message does not exist
│  └─ Go back to the input to confirm whether it really follows the message path
├─ Message exists but user adjacency is not visible
│  └─ Save the input shape and stop at the message decoding boundary
└─ User adjacency is visible
   └─ For now, treat the identity fields as already present in the object
```

At the time, "input shape" only meant whether the object at hand was a message container, a user inside a message, or still of unidentified origin. It was not a request to fill in a fixed set of fields, much less to create a message wrapper just to get through the tree. When no message exists in the first place, first confirm whether upstream is supposed to provide one; without that prerequisite, an empty message cannot be treated as an identity field failure.

The early record had one practical benefit: it prevented several impulses to immediately classify an empty object as a deserialization issue. When even the message container does not exist, there is no point continuing to infer field results from user adjacency. This stopping point is still retained. The mistake was subsequently treating "user adjacency is visible" as a stopping point as well; the two are not the same kind of judgment.

## The Margin Rule at the Time

A sentence had been left in the blank space on the old page:

> If the user object inside the message is not null, assume for now that the identity fields have no compatibility issues.

This sentence is now marked **deprecated**. It is not entirely unfounded: in the message path at the time, a missing user object was indeed a branch that needed to be handled first. But it compressed the object's existence, the correctness of the read result, and the completeness of the object's output into a single sentence. When a user object is passed directly, this rule does not even have a suitable entry point.

The original sentence is retained to show why the old troubleshooting process often started with `Message`, and to avoid presenting the order corrected later as a conclusion that had existed from the beginning. The old entry point can still be used to identify the message source; the old stop condition cannot continue to be used to end the identity-field review.

The old tree also contained an unstated assumption: as long as the input passed through a message container, reading and writing out the identity object would occur at the same observable location. This assumption was not supported by object samples from that time. It was merely a convenient lookup order, not proof of the object relationship. Only after the possibility of a direct object arose did it become clear that this underlying assumption also needed to be separated from the tree.

## 2023-11-27: The two sides that did not line up during review

A later review encountered a more specific point of confusion: the object log showed a numeric value, but there was not enough output evidence to establish whether JSON still retained the corresponding attribute. Someone first suspected that the message object had been replaced after decoding, because the message path was the first code entry point found at the time. This assumption did not narrow the scope.

It could not explain the report in which a user object was obtained directly, nor explain how two observations could occur at different locations: "the read operation returned a value" and "the attribute was missing when it was written out again." The bigger issue is the review did not retain the complete original input. Without the input, it was impossible to determine whether `id` was absent from the input, the decoded value was different, or serialization failed to retain the attribute. Therefore, the field type was not changed at that time, nor was a specific result inferred from the annotation in the file header.

After the review, the recording method was changed to preserve three sections side by side:

1. Whether the original input exists and whether it contains `id`;
2. What is obtained after performing the read operation on the identity object;
3. Whether JSON still carries `id` after being output again.

This is not a complete call chain. It only covers the observable material near the object boundary. How the caller subsequently stores, compares, or converts the identifier is not to be filled in by guesswork on this page. If all three sections are normal but the upper layer still reports a discrepancy, the evidence should be taken back to the actual call site for further checking.

If the input is not a message container, do not fabricate an extra `Message` layer and continue. When a direct object comes in, first save its input shape, then record the read result; only when the message source is explicit should you additionally note whether a message exists and whether user adjacency is visible. An empty message does not automatically mean the identity field is abnormal, and visible user adjacency does not automatically mean the round trip was successful.

There was once an easily misread blank in the review checklist: the output fragment was not saved, which does not mean the output side had already failed. That column at the time only indicated that a comparison could not be made. Later, "output unknown" was added instead of "serialization error" so that the next investigator would not continue searching annotations along a nonexistent error. Importing annotations from the message file can help confirm the reading location, but cannot fill in the missing output material.

## An Attribution That Did Not Hold

During the compatibility consolidation period, newly added capability fields were also changing. Because they occurred close together in time, someone treated this as the cause of the identity-field change and wanted to start with the capability fields to explain the difference. Later, no object fragment was found that could link the two in a direct causal relationship.

This attempt is recorded as a failed working hypothesis, not as the current branch. Capability fields and identity fields can appear at the same time, and can also be observed on the same object; existing records do not support a claim such as "the newly added capability fields overwrote the identity fields." For inputs where capability fields appear, still inspect the identity read and JSON output separately; do not skip the basic comparison just because the object is richer.

Here too, do not treat a missing capability field as evidence of an identity anomaly. It is a neighboring compatibility issue; unless the incident materials simultaneously show differences in the identity field's input, read, or output, do not tie the two together on this page.

At the time, we did not adopt the approach of "remove the newly added capability fields first and then inspect the identity value." It would change the object's shape, but could not answer where the read value actually came from, nor restore the missing input and output fragments. Even if the report disappeared after removing unrelated fields, that would not show which side had originally had the problem. This attempt stopped at the candidate stage and did not become an on-call action.

## 2025-04-30: The Counterexample Changed the First Question

During later cleanup, the counterexample that remained was small: a minimal identity object need not be attached to a message; a read operation returning a number cannot substitute for checking the re-emitted property. This counterexample does not require moving all JSON fields into the troubleshooting tree, yet it is enough to overturn the old rule.

Therefore, the first question was changed to "What is the input source?" rather than defaulting to the message branch. When it is clear that the input came from a message, the message container and user adjacency are ancillary facts; when it is clearly a direct object, there is no need to look back for a nonexistent message; when the source is unknown, do not force a classification just because the old documentation starts with messages.

This change also corrected a wording choice in old records. "No Message" was often recorded as an anomaly; it should now first be split into two cases: the material was originally supposed to carry a message but did not, or the material was a direct identity object to begin with. For the former, it is still valid to stop at the message-decoding boundary; the latter should not enter that boundary. Writing both as "message missing" loses the earliest branch, namely the input source.

For a minimal object, minimality is not a recipe specifying which business fields remain after trimming, but a requirement that identity fields must still be observable on their own when no additional capability information is available in the current environment to explain the differences. It provides a boundary for counterexamples, without requiring the investigator to devise a new construction method. If only in-message objects are available in the current environment, they can also be documented under the message branch; the message path must simply not be mistaken for the sole prerequisite.

## 2025-05-01: Review excerpts

The review retained two short statements:

> `Message` is an easy-to-find entry point, not the root node of all identity objects.
>
> Having a user object only means that you can continue checking; record the read result and the output result separately.

These two statements correct the troubleshooting order, rather than adding responsibilities to `Message`. The declarations and annotation imports in the file are still useful starting points for reading the code; they cannot replace the input and output artifacts for a minimal object.

The review also changed "a numeric value is visible in the object log" from a pass condition to an intermediate observation. Numeric values in the log can help document the read side, but cannot substitute for the presence of the input field, nor for JSON being output again. Conversely, seeing `id` in the output only shows that the output has that property, and does not establish that the read operation necessarily returned the same identifier. Only after retaining results from both sides can you hand off the discrepancy for investigation outside the object boundary.

The review did not require preserving the caller's entire state. If the caller still reports an inconsistency and the input, read, and output records are already complete, just bring back those three records. How the caller stores or compares identifiers is a separate troubleshooting entry point; the location of the message class, annotation names, or object logs cannot be used on this page to infer that behavior.

## Reordering the on-call branches

The tree below is a version added alongside the old tree. It starts with observable symptoms, and each branch has an explicit stopping point. When samples cannot be obtained, do not fill in the gaps with "it should be working normally".

```text
Identity field compatibility review
│
├─ Does the input come from Message?
│  ├─ Yes
│  │  ├─ Message is missing or the adjacent user is not visible
│  │  │  └─ Save the input shape and stop at the message decoding boundary
│  │  └─ Message is available
│  │     └─ Continue checking the values read from the user object and the JSON output
│  └─ No or cannot confirm
│     └─ Do not enter the message branch, check the identity object directly
│
├─ Does the input include id?
│  ├─ No
│  │  └─ Stop on the input side and record the missing field
│  └─ Yes
│     └─ Compare the input field with the value read after decoding
│
├─ Is the value read abnormal?
│  ├─ Yes
│  │  └─ Stop at the decoding boundary and save the input and the value read
│  └─ No
│     └─ Proceed to the JSON output, do not stop just because the value read is normal
│
└─ Does the JSON output retain id?
   ├─ No
   │  └─ Save the output excerpt and stay on the serialization side
   ├─ Yes, but the caller still reports a discrepancy
   │  └─ Return to the call site with evidence from the input, the read and the output
   └─ Cannot obtain the output
      └─ Mark the review as incomplete and draw no round-trip conclusion
```

The first level of the tree does not require first proving that the message object "should exist". It only asks whether the current evidence actually comes from the message path. If the input is clearly a direct identity object, inspect that object directly; if the input source is unclear, the message path is only a possibility that remains to be confirmed. Older records often described "no message" as an anomaly, but the absence of a message should now be distinguished from not taking the message path in the first place.

The second level separates missing input from object behavior. When the raw input lacks `id`, subsequent object logs cannot fill that gap, and the record should stop on the input side. Only when the raw input contains `id` but the value read differs should the review stop at the decoding boundary. The conclusion here does not change based on whether the message is empty, because message state cannot replace a field comparison.

The third level prevents a common shortcut: stopping after reading a numeric value. If a read operation can return a numeric value, that only means an observable result is still available on the read side; it does not validate the JSON that is output again. Conversely, seeing a property in the output does not prove that the value read is the expected identifier after decoding. Evidence must be retained separately for both sides.

The final level separates serialization gaps from caller discrepancies. When the value read is normal but the output does not contain `id`, keep the record on the serialization side, rather than going back to explain it with "the adjacent user is visible". When the input, the value read and the output all match expectations but the caller still reports an inconsistency, do not record the caller state as a field of `Message` either; the only option is to return to the actual boundary with all three sets of evidence.

### Recording order for the message branch

Confirm that the material came from a message; there is no need to copy the entire message object into the record. First record whether the message container exists; when the container exists, then record whether user adjacency is visible; these two items only help explain how the identity object arrived at the scene. Then continue using the three sections: input, read, and output. If user adjacency is not visible, stop the record near message decoding; do not write that the identity field has been lost.

For direct objects, the two message items have no applicable place. Do not add a "message not visible" line just because the old tree starts from `Message`. For a direct object, whether the raw input has `id`, what the read operation obtains, and whether the output retains the attribute are already sufficient to form a local record. The same applies when the source is unknown: preserve "source unknown" first; do not infer from the file path that the input must be a message.

### When the output cannot be obtained

Unavailable output is a stopping condition, not a small gap that can be covered by the read value. When recording the read side, you can state whether the numeric value matches the input; but without an output fragment, you cannot mark the object's write-out behavior as normal. Some previous old entries left "the object looks normal" as the conclusion, making it difficult later to determine whether this referred to reading or writing; this is also why the three sections are separated.

Only when the output fragment has been obtained and `id` is absent should the issue remain on the serialization side. Do not directly select one explanation based on the presence of `JsonIgnore`, `JsonIgnoreProperties`, or `JsonProperty`; this page does not contain enough material to determine the scope of the specific annotation's effect. Leave both the input and output sides as they are, and avoid turning navigation clues into attribution.

## A checklist that is still useful but already outdated

Below is the message-first checklist often cited by old entry points. It is kept here because when someone encounters message input, the first few items can still be used to quickly organize the situation; the fourth item no longer applies.

1. Open `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/message/Message.java` and confirm that the material at hand really involves message-model adjacency.
2. When the message is not visible, go back to the input and retrieve the original fields; do not create a message wrapper out of thin air.
3. When the message is visible, record whether user adjacency is visible.
4. ~~Stop as soon as user adjacency is visible.~~
5. When the object log contains a numeric value, still obtain the JSON output.

Items 1 through 3 apply only to message sources. Item 4 was overturned by the later minimal-object counterexample, and the strikethrough is retained so readers arriving from the old page can see that the stopping point has changed. Item 5 comes from the review in which "a value was read, but the output was not checked" and still applies to both message and direct-object sources.

The old checklist did not require preserving the full caller state, nor should it be expanded into an audit of all JSON fields. If the object at hand is not a message, simply skip items 1 through 3; do not disguise a direct object as a user inside a message just to reuse the old page.

## Correction Regarding the File Entry Point

There was another early conclusion: "The message declaration can be found in the file, so the identity field implementation is in the message class." This statement is also marked as not applicable. The declaration of `Message` only indicates that the message model is located there; you cannot infer the full implementation of the user fields or responsibility for serialization from its location.

This correction does not mean the message file has no value. It remains a stable entry point for examining the message path and can also help confirm whether the current discussion concerns a message container or a direct object. What has changed is how it should be used: treat it as a navigation aid, not as establishing ownership of everything. Forcing reports about direct identity objects into searches of the message class often only prolongs troubleshooting.

The three Jackson annotation imports at the top of the file are also retained as clues when reading the code, not as conclusions. The old notes linked them to "identity fields are handled within the message class"; they should now be written separately: the former is visible text, while the latter requires evidence from the input, read results, or output to be established. This distinction may seem subtle, but it can prevent modifying the model directly when no sample is available.

## Current Requirements

The current review retains only one explicit requirement for the minimal identity object: `User.getId()` must return the decoded long identifier for the minimal identity object, serialization must still output the `id` property, and this behavior must not drift because of newly added capability fields.

This requirement applies only to the read and round-trip behavior of the minimal identity object and does not change the branching by input source. When the user comes from a message, still record whether the message container and user adjacency are visible; when the user comes in directly, do not add a message to the record. The presence of capability fields is not a reason to skip identity checks either; still examine the read result and the written JSON separately.

When following the current tree, specify the stopping point precisely: if the input lacks `id`, stop on the input side; if the input contains `id` but the read result differs, stop on the decoding side; if the read result is normal but the output lacks `id`, stop on the serialization side; if all three sets of evidence meet expectations but the caller still reports an inconsistency, stop at the caller boundary. This page has no evidence for the last case, so do not infer how the caller stores the identifier.

## Adjacent issues not yet split out

A call to Fang Ke can write its own state after reading the identifier, and only then compare the object output and report differences. The available material does not establish whether the issue occurs during object reading, object output, or after the caller saves it. For reports of this kind, collect only whether the input contains `id`, what the read operation returns, and whether JSON retains `id`; include the message object's state only when the message source is clear, and leave it unknown if the source is unclear.

Likewise, there is no material showing whether the caller relies on the ordering of fields in JSON. Do not feed this unresolved point back into the object compatibility rules, nor infer caller behavior from annotations in the message file.

## Old example appendix: Message-first stopping points

The old example did not retain the complete input, so only the sequence recorded at the time can be reconstructed: first confirm that `Message` was visible, then confirm that user adjacency was visible, then copy a numeric value from the object log. That record contains no JSON output, nor does it state whether the object was read from within the message or passed separately afterward. The old example therefore cannot serve as a sample of current round-trip behavior.

Two points can still be gleaned from it. First, the process does not continue guessing from user adjacency when the message container is missing, and this stopping point is retained. Second, the process ends immediately once user adjacency is visible, but this stopping point is no longer valid. Do not fabricate the original JSON alongside the old example, nor retroactively add a direct-object counterexample that did not exist at the time; it serves only as a trace of why message-first troubleshooting was retained.

## Outstanding items at the end of the page

- Paired samples of direct input and input within a message for the minimal identity object have not yet been recorded on this page.
- As for an exception in which the presence or absence of the newly added capability field affects only a particular construction path, none has been confirmed here.
- Whether the re-output JSON has already been retained, when the caller reports differences, still depends on the material available from the incident.

The old tree preserved the message entry point, the follow-up verification notes separated reading from output, and the review counterexample eliminated "stop once the object is visible". Together these records explain why this page is still being pulled up from the old path; but current judgments should follow the later branches and the current requirements.

# Default Telegram Endpoint Decision Record

This page started as a narrowly scoped decision left over from wrapping up compatibility work. The default Telegram endpoint was often casually called the "client address," while custom endpoints were easily folded into the same discussion. The initial draft kept them separate because there wasn't enough material then to establish where the default value came from or whether the caller had any part in selecting the address.

The initial draft laid out three approaches: attribute the behavior to the caller not overriding the address; trace upward from the OkHttp client; or first consolidate the default and custom addresses into a single write-up. The second was chosen. The first assumed that the caller participated in the selection; the third would have turned speculation into a convention. The decision retained was not "the client holds the endpoint," but to start reading the code at the client object.

At the time, someone narrowed the scope based on `HttpUrl` appearing in the file and left a verbal assessment that "the default Telegram address is probably handled here." That assessment should no longer be treated as an implementation description. Importing the URL type only shows that the file references that type; it neither confirms where the default address is defined nor tells us at which layer an override occurs.

This page records a somewhat awkward verification history. The issue was named "Video Covers and Start Times", but the earlier investigation record led people to a poll method file. The file does exist, and the path is specific enough, but those two points did not automatically add up to a single fact. Later revisions did not gloss over this awkwardness, but instead made it the starting point for the decision on this page.

The path is preserved exactly as follows:

`telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/methods/polls/SendPoll.java`

It is located in:

`org.telegram.telegrambots.meta.api.methods.polls`

The following declarations are directly visible in the file header:

```java
package org.telegram.telegrambots.meta.api.methods.polls;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonIgnoreProperties;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import lombok.AllArgsConstructor;
```

These lines serve two practical purposes. First, anyone revisiting the investigation can confirm that they have opened the local reference point left by the earlier investigation, rather than finding another file based on a similar issue name. Second, the review can start from the file's own package declaration and direct dependencies, without treating the issue title as a code index. Beyond that, these lines do not serve as evidence for anything further.

`JsonIgnoreProperties`, `JsonProperty`, and `AllArgsConstructor` are dependency names visible in the file header. No annotation targets, member lists, serialization samples, or caller results have been frozen here, so these dependencies cannot be used as a basis for filling in video cover fields or explaining how the playback start time enters a request or a returned result. Connecting these three dependencies into a complete behavioral chain would make a local observation look like an implementation description.

The problem left by the earlier investigation is not just that "the wrong file may have been found". More specifically, it collapsed four levels into a single pointer: the issue name, the file path, the file declarations, and the result seen by the user. The issue name can indicate where the search started; the path can preserve navigation coordinates; the declarations can show what is actually in the file header; the user-visible result must be obtained from the states before and after the operation. The actual reference relationships still need to be checked against the saved revision. None of these four levels can substitute for another.

## Working Hypothesis from the Initial Draft

The initial draft adopted a very narrow working hypothesis: the issue name and call name can lead people to `SendPoll.java`, but cannot by themselves prove that this file is where the video compatibility behavior is implemented. This hypothesis was not written as "the problem is elsewhere", nor as "the file is unrelated to the issue". It only separates name-based navigation from implementation attribution.

The three approaches considered at the time were as follows:

| Approach | What it could provide at the time | Costs involved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record `SendPoll.java` as the definitive implementation location | The page would quickly have a clear answer | May mistake being pointed to for being responsible for the implementation, leading subsequent diff work to focus on the wrong target |
| Continue expanding the search by issue name and call name | More entry points with similar names | More names do not mean the reference relationships have been verified, and the uncertainty will keep being carried forward |
| Keep the file entry point fixed, recheck the before-and-after states, then check the actual references | Preserve both navigation and the sequence of events as observed | Fields, callers, and the complete behavioral chain cannot be filled in yet |

The decision was to adopt the third option. It is not a new API design, and it has not changed any interface behavior. It only determines how object boundaries are preserved in this history when the available material is insufficient: paths may be included in the record, but conclusions must not be broadened until they are supported by direct references or resulting states.

This trade-off seemed conservative at first. For readers, opening a specific Java file but seeing no video fields can create the impression that "something may have been left out". But if package names, imports, and the issue title are pieced together to establish field ownership, the page will appear more complete than the facts warrant, and it will be harder during revisions to identify where the error began. Here, it is preferable to leave the gap visible rather than fill it with an object that has no source.

## Distinctions retained after the review

The verification separated "a clear entry point" and "a clear relationship" into two different things. A clear entry point means the old record provides a path that can be opened; a clear relationship means the actual references in that path can connect changes in the user's environment to objects in the file. The current material reliably supports only the former, while the latter still needs investigation.

"Visible file header" and "visible behavior" must likewise be kept separate. The package declaration and the three imports are observations from the file header. They show that the file resides in the corresponding directory of the existing module and uses the listed declaration tools. Visible behavior, on the other hand, requires examining what happens before and after a call; the presence of `JsonProperty` cannot substitute for JSON results, nor can the presence of `JsonIgnoreProperties` substitute for a conclusion about how unknown fields are handled.

"A change occurred" and "ownership is settled" must also be kept separate. Even if a change in the video cover or playback start time is observed during verification, it can initially only be recorded as a result observed in the user's environment; whether that change occurred during preparation, request construction, remote processing, or result reading still requires further assessment based on references and local objects. Conversely, even if a similar declaration is found in the file, the before-and-after states in the user's environment cannot be skipped to write it up directly as a change the user has already seen.

These distinctions are the substantive content retained in this revision, not formatting reminders. They explain why this page preserves both a source-code entry point and a verification step in the user's environment: the former answers "where to go back and look", the latter answers "what changes must be confirmed first", and only together do they provide enough support for the next focused verification.

The path of `SendPoll.java` provides three usable coordinates. It is in the existing Java module under `telegrambots-meta`; it belongs to the `api.methods.polls` package path; it is the specific file left by the earlier investigation, not a directory guessed anew from the issue name. If these details cannot be linked back to the results observed in the environment, the page can still be useful: it preserves the coordinates for verification and the boundaries that were not crossed at the time.

The revision has not watered this statement down into a generic interface principle, but has instead added its specific consequences in three places: paths can serve as navigation, file headers can serve as local observations, and behavior attribution must be advanced through both actual references and the state observed in the user's environment.

# Copy Button and Inline Field Proposal

To wrap this up, we're putting "Copy Text Inline Keyboard Button" and "Prepared Inline Message Boolean Fields" through the same API review, but not treating them as a single field change. The former is an entry point for user actions; the latter represents state for prepared inline messages. If we judge them only by whether the JSON property can be read, it's easy to miss how one of the two is used.

The initial proposal is to keep the two objects in their respective model locations, then decide whether a shared regression sample is needed. Message is at `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/message/Message.java`, and its currently visible declaration is `public class Message implements MaybeInaccessibleMessage {`. It is a useful reference for checking existing annotation conventions around the message object, but that should not be taken to mean that Message contains both new objects.

The review needs to compare three approaches:

- Only add model fields, relying on standard object round trips for coverage;
- Keep separate samples for the copy button and the boolean field, then have callers check usability;
- Combine them into a single message-level sample first, then split it later.

The third approach reduces maintenance work, but would conflate whether the button's copy action works with whether the boolean state takes effect, creating a single failure surface. It is not recommended as the default path at this stage. The first approach also isn't enough to show that the state of prepared inline messages is actually used.

Still undecided: whether the copy button needs a separate everyday-use sample; which actual CI run should record the boolean field's runtime result; whether the two samples can share a single regression entry point. If we later confirm that either object can only be verified through a separate path, we'll drop the idea of combining the samples.

# Copy Button and Inline Field Proposal

The May draft put the two objects side by side to avoid closing out the interface with only a generic "message fields added" assessment. That rationale still stands after review, but the proposal is narrower: this covers arrangements for regression samples and interface verification. It does not treat the message object's path as proof of implementation ownership or assume that any existing sample already covers the new semantics.

The original shortcut was to put both Copy Text Inline Keyboard Button and Prepared Inline Message Boolean Fields in the same message sample and use successful serialization and deserialization as the pass criteria for this round. This remains a fallback, not the preferred option. It would leave the failure output unable to answer a simple question: did the button fail to enter the normal usage flow, or did the boolean field fail to actually take effect after processing? Having both in the same sample does not mean they share an interface boundary.

## Objects to Check Separately First

Copy Text Inline Keyboard Button needs an object representation that callers can use. Its check should focus not on "whether the button-related JSON contains a block of text," but on whether the sample actually reaches the inline keyboard path that the copy action depends on. Checking only static configuration would mistakenly treat it as integrated even when a usage entry point is missing.

Prepared Inline Message Boolean Fields, by contrast, should be checked based on its state after processing. The field's presence in the object only proves that the model has a place for it; the result of an actual CI run is required to determine whether it takes effect. The draft treated a normal object round trip as potential evidence. It is now retained only as a basic check: if the round trip fails, fix the model or mapping first; if it succeeds but the runtime state is wrong, the field cannot be considered complete.

This distinction also affects how the samples are written. The copy button sample does not need to cover every state combination for prepared inline messages, and the boolean field sample should not rely on the button's presence to prove it is usable. If a call path later really does need both, a combined sample can be added; a combined sample can only supplement interaction coverage, not replace the minimal checks for each object.

## Possible Arrangements

**Option A: Keep a minimal sample for each.**

Keep a check for the copy button that exercises the normal usage flow; keep a runtime check for the boolean field that makes its post-processing state observable. Confine the shared parts to the existing model round-trip checks. This makes the failure boundaries clear, at the cost of maintaining two sample descriptions with different semantics.

**Option B: One combined sample.**

Put the two objects in the same message-related sample and check construction, encoding, and decoding together. This is useful early on for establishing whether both objects can be represented together, but does not provide enough evidence to assess runtime state. If this is the only sample retained, later issues will require splitting them apart again to diagnose the cause, so it is not recommended as the sole basis for release.

**Option C: Check only model declarations.**

This option is the easiest to complete and the most likely to leave gaps. The location of the Message file can help navigate nearby code: in `telegrambots-meta/src/main/java/org/telegram/telegrambots/meta/api/objects/message/Message.java`, `public class Message implements MaybeInaccessibleMessage {` is one of the entry points for checking message objects. The file already imports `JsonIgnore`, `JsonIgnoreProperties`, and `JsonProperty` at the top, so the existing annotation style can be reviewed here; but those local declarations alone cannot settle field placement, state handling, or caller-visible effects for the two objects. Option C is therefore suitable only as a starting point for reading the code.

The preference this round is Option A; a short combined sample may be added as a troubleshooting aid. "Keeping separate samples" does not mean two full sets of end-to-end coverage are required: the copy button sample only needs to prove that the normal usage entry point is reached, and the boolean field sample only needs to tie the post-run state assessment to an actual CI run. There is no need to add the same number of cases on both sides just for symmetry.

## Changes to the Old Draft

The old draft proposed deciding first whether the two samples could share a regression entry point. "Sharing" is no longer the starting point. A safer sequence is to determine what each object lacks, then see whether an existing entry point can accommodate both.

Another change concerns how Message is used. The draft listed it as a possible home for both objects, which could lead readers to take the source path as a conclusion. After review, only two explicit uses remain: inspecting the objects and annotations adjacent to `Message`; and using it as a starting point for tracing back when a model check fails. Whether the copy button and Prepared Inline Message Boolean Fields belong directly in this class still needs to be confirmed against actual references.

Investigations related to unknown fields are documented separately in DOC-23. That page covers unknown-field tolerance in CopyMessage; do not use the observation that unknown properties are ignored as a substitute for the button usage checks or boolean state checks here. Both topics may involve object decoding, but they focus on different things.

## Exit Conditions and Open Items

If any of the following occurs, drop the idea that "a combined sample can help with regression testing" and return to an arrangement that keeps them completely separate:

- The combined sample can only confirm an object round trip and cannot show the post-processing state of Prepared Inline Message Boolean Fields;
- Copy Text Inline Keyboard Button appears in the combined path, but the normal usage flow is not reached;
- A single failure masks both the button and the state field, and the CI output cannot distinguish which side to fix first.

The following remain unconfirmed: what kind of result an actual CI run should record to be sufficient to show that the field takes effect; whether a reusable entry point already exists for the copy button's caller-side sample; and whether the combined sample would introduce message fields unrelated to these two objects. Until these are confirmed, do not use the existence of a configuration file or a single JSON round trip as a substitute for a runtime assessment.

If subsequent changes only add model declarations, note here that the gap in runtime checks remains unchanged; if they include an actual CI run, attach the results under the boolean field check, rather than going back and rewriting the May draft to state that the work is complete.
